meta.titre: Storm Hydrographs: reading the shape of a flood and explaining lag time

sections.contenu_markdown: During the rainy season, heavy rain over paved areas of a city like Douala can send water to the streams and drains within hours, causing flash floods, while a river draining a large forested area rises slowly. Hydrologists record this on a storm hydrograph. Examiners ask you to read a graph, to calculate the lag time, to recognise the type of hydrograph from its description and to explain how the features of a basin change its shape. This course gives the vocabulary, the factors and a method for each type of question.

items: A drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries.
Discharge is the volume of water passing a point in a river each second, measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs).
Infiltration is the movement of water into the soil, and surface runoff is water flowing over the ground.
A gauging station is a place where river level and discharge are measured.

sections.titre: Storm hydrographs: features, types and controlling factors
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms
- **Storm (flood) hydrograph**: a graph of river discharge, in cubic metres per second (cumecs), against time at one point, usually a gauging station, during and after a rainstorm.
- **Base flow**: the normal flow supplied by groundwater. **Storm flow** (quickflow): the extra flow from rainwater reaching the channel by surface runoff and throughflow.
- **Rising limb**: the part of the curve where discharge increases as runoff arrives. **Peak discharge**: the highest point. **Falling (recession) limb**: the part where discharge decreases.
- **Lag time**: the time between the peak of the rainfall and the peak of the discharge.

### Reading the shape
| Type | Rising limb | Peak | Falling limb | Lag time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flashy | Steep | High and short | Steep | Short |
| Intermediate | Moderately steep | Moderate | Moderate | Medium |
| Subdued (gentle) | Gentle | Low and flat or prolonged | Very gentle | Long |

Always read the description of the three parts (rising limb, peak, falling limb) before choosing the type.

### Static (long-term) factors that control lag time and peak
| Factor | Short lag, sharp peak | Long lag, low peak |
|---|---|---|
| Basin size | Small basin: water has a short distance to travel | Large basin: water from far away arrives later |
| Basin shape | Circular: tributaries deliver water together | Elongated: arrival is spread over time |
| Drainage density | High: many streams carry water quickly | Low: water moves slowly |
| Slope | Steep: fast runoff | Gentle: slower runoff |
| Rock and soil | Impermeable (clay, granite): surface runoff | Permeable: infiltration and slow throughflow |
| Land use | Urban areas, bare ground | Dense vegetation delays water by interception and infiltration |

**Dynamic factors** change from storm to storm: rainfall intensity and duration, how wet the soil already is, season and temperature. Heavy rain on saturated ground produces more runoff and a higher, sharper peak.

variantes.nom: How static factors influence lag time at the gauging station
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks how permanent characteristics of a drainage basin affect lag time.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose three or four factors. For each, name the factor, say whether it shortens or lengthens the lag time, and give the reason in terms of the speed and distance of water movement. Example: a high drainage density gives many channels, so rainwater reaches the main river quickly and the lag time is short.

variantes.nom: Explain a sharp or a gentle hydrograph from basin size, shape or land use
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a diagram or description shows two hydrographs and asks why they differ.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Describe the difference (peak height, lag, limb steepness), then explain with distance travelled, arrival time of water from different parts of the basin, infiltration and storage. A small basin gives water a short route and nearly simultaneous arrival, so the peak is sharp; a large basin spreads arrival over time and gives a lower, broader peak.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The discharge of a river at a gauging station is recorded each hour after a storm whose rainfall peaked at 10:00.

| Time | 08:00 | 09:00 | 10:00 | 11:00 | 12:00 | 13:00 | 14:00 | 15:00 | 16:00 | 17:00 | 18:00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discharge (m³/s) | 5 | 5 | 6 | 14 | 38 | 52 | 41 | 26 | 15 | 9 | 6 |

(a) State the base flow and the peak discharge. (b) Calculate the lag time. (c) Calculate the average rate of rise of the rising limb between 10:00 and the peak. (d) Describe the hydrograph and give two possible static factors.

etapes.action: Read the base flow and the peak.
etapes.justification: Base flow is the steady discharge before the storm arrives; the peak is the highest value.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Base flow about 5 to 6 m³/s; peak discharge 52 m³/s at 13:00.

etapes.justification: Lag time = time of peak discharge minus time of peak rainfall.
Rate = change in discharge divided by time.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Discharge rises from 6 m³/s at 10:00 to 52 m³/s at 13:00: $\frac{52 - 6}{3} = 15.3$ m³/s per hour.

etapes.action: Calculate the rate of fall for comparison.
etapes.justification: Compare the two limbs to describe the shape.
etapes.resultat_markdown: From 52 m³/s at 13:00 to 6 m³/s at 18:00: $\frac{52 - 6}{5} = 9.2$ m³/s per hour.

etapes.justification: State the features, then link to the basin.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The peak is nearly nine times the base flow, the rising limb is steeper than the falling limb and the lag time is moderate. Likely static factors: a medium-sized basin with fairly high drainage density, and impermeable soils or some built-up land.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Base flow about 5 to 6 m³/s, peak 52 m³/s, lag time 3 hours, rate of rise about 15.3 m³/s per hour.** The hydrograph is moderately flashy: a steep rising limb, a moderate peak and a falling limb that is gentler than the rise. Static factors such as basin size, drainage density and impermeable surfaces explain the short to moderate lag time.

items.erreur_markdown: Defining lag time as the time from the start of rain to the end of the flood.
items.pourquoi_faux: Lag time is measured from the peak of the rainfall to the peak of the discharge.
items.correction_markdown: Write: lag time = time of peak discharge minus time of peak rainfall.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing a large basin as having a shorter lag time because "it has more water".
items.pourquoi_faux: In a larger basin, water from distant parts needs longer to reach the gauging station, so lag time is longer and the peak lower.
items.correction_markdown: Link size to distance travelled and the time of arrival of water.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing rainfall intensity and antecedent soil moisture as static factors.
items.pourquoi_faux: These change from one storm to the next, so they are dynamic factors. Static factors are permanent features such as size, shape, drainage density and rock type.
items.correction_markdown: Use basin size, shape, slope, geology, drainage density and long-term land use as static factors.

items.erreur_markdown: Choosing a hydrograph type from the peak alone.
items.pourquoi_faux: The type depends on the rising limb, the duration of the peak and the falling limb together, and on the lag time.
items.correction_markdown: Match each described feature before choosing.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that urbanisation lengthens the lag time because "there is more water".
items.pourquoi_faux: Paved surfaces and drains reduce infiltration and carry water quickly to rivers, so lag time shortens and the peak rises.
items.correction_markdown: Write that impermeable surfaces increase runoff and speed it up, giving a flashier hydrograph.

items.enonce_markdown: On a rainy day the heaviest rainfall in a basin occurs at 09:30 and the river reaches its highest discharge at 12:00. Define lag time and calculate it. State what shape of hydrograph you expect if the lag time is short.
items.solution_markdown: **Lag time** is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. 12:00 minus 09:30 gives **2.5 hours**. A short lag time gives a flashy hydrograph: steep rising limb, high sharp peak and steep falling limb.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) At a gauging station the river channel is 15 m wide with an average depth of 2 m and a mean velocity of 1.2 m/s. Calculate the discharge. (b) Basin A has 150 km of streams in an area of 60 km²; basin B has 66 km of streams in an area of 60 km². Calculate the drainage density of each and say which is likely to have the shorter lag time.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Discharge = width x depth x velocity $= 15 \times 2 \times 1.2 = 36$ m³/s. (b) Drainage density = total stream length divided by area. A: $\frac{150}{60} = 2.5$ km per km². B: $\frac{66}{60} = 1.1$ km per km². **Discharge 36 m³/s; A has the higher drainage density (2.5 against 1.1), so water reaches the main channel faster and A is likely to have the shorter lag time and a sharper peak.**

items.enonce_markdown: Before a town was built in a basin, a storm produced a peak discharge of 20 m³/s with a lag time of 6 hours. After building, a similar storm produced a peak of 55 m³/s with a lag time of 2 hours. (a) Calculate the change in lag time and in peak discharge as percentages of the original values. (b) Explain the changes.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Lag time fell by $6 - 2 = 4$ hours, which is $\frac{4}{6} \times 100 = 67$ per cent. Peak discharge rose by $55 - 20 = 35$ m³/s, which is $\frac{35}{20} \times 100 = 175$ per cent. (b) Roofs, roads and car parks are impermeable, so infiltration and storage fall and surface runoff rises; gutters and drains carry water quickly to the river; vegetation that intercepted rain is removed. Water therefore reaches the channel faster and in greater volume. **Lag time down 67 per cent; peak discharge up 175 per cent; the hydrograph is flashier.**

items_markdown: A storm hydrograph plots discharge against time; its parts are base flow, rising limb, peak, falling limb and lag time.
Lag time = time of peak discharge minus time of peak rainfall.
Flashy hydrograph: steep limbs, high peak, short lag time. Subdued hydrograph: gentle limbs, low peak, long lag time.
Static factors include basin size and shape, drainage density, slope, geology, soil and land use. Dynamic factors include rainfall intensity and antecedent moisture.
Small, circular, steep, impermeable or urban basins give short lag times and sharp peaks; large, elongated, permeable or vegetated basins give long lag times and low peaks.
